candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — bed-exit alarms and fall prevention
candidate.educational_objective: Explain that bed-exit alarms are monitoring/alerting tools rather than physical restraints and should not replace individualized fall-risk assessment and prevention planning.

options.A: The alarm mechanically restrains the client in bed and therefore replaces other individualized fall-prevention interventions.
options.B: The alarm alerts staff when the client begins to move or attempts to exit the bed; it does not physically prevent bed exit and should be used only as part of an individualized fall-prevention plan when appropriate.
options.C: The alarm locks the bed rails in place and prevents voluntary movement until a nurse deactivates the device.
options.D: Once activated, the alarm eliminates fall risk, so ongoing reassessment and a tailored prevention plan are unnecessary.

candidate.rationale: AHRQ describes bed alarms as alerting devices that notify staff when a patient attempts to get out of bed. Current AHRQ fall-prevention resources emphasize formal risk assessment and a tailored plan rather than one-size-fits-all reliance on alarms. Therefore B is correct: the alarm signals movement/exit attempts but does not physically restrain the client or eliminate fall risk. A, C, and D incorrectly treat an alerting device as a restraint or complete prevention strategy.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Bed alarms alert staff to attempted bed exit rather than physically restraining the patient; fall prevention should be individualized and layered rather than relying on alarms alone.
